title: PCOS Is Now PMOS: What the New Name Means for Women's Diagnosis
excerpt: A global medical consensus published in The Lancet in May 2026 has renamed polycystic ovary syndrome as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome — a shift experts say could speed up diagnosis and ease stigma for the 170 million women affected.
body:
• Polycystic ovary syndrome is now officially polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), following a global consensus published in The Lancet on May 12, 2026 and endorsed by 56 medical organizations.
  • The rename corrects a misleading label: roughly 30% of patients don't have ovarian cysts, and the condition is a whole-body hormonal and metabolic disorder, not an ovary-only one.
  • Diagnosis and treatment are unchanged — lifestyle measures, metformin and hormonal contraceptives remain first-line — but doctors are expected to screen for metabolic risks earlier.
  • What women should do: existing diagnoses and prescriptions stand, with no new tests or paperwork needed; at your next check-up, ask whether insulin resistance and metabolic screening (blood sugar, lipids, blood pressure) are part of your care plan.

One of the most common conditions in women's health has a new name. Polycystic ovary syndrome — PCOS — is now officially polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, or PMOS, after a global consensus published in The Lancet on May 12, 2026 and endorsed by 56 international medical organizations and patient groups. It affects roughly 170 million women of reproductive age worldwide, and an estimated 4 to 22.5 percent of women in India. Experts say the change goes well beyond semantics: it could speed up diagnosis, reshape treatment conversations and ease decades of stigma.

Why the old name had to go

The problem was in the first word. "Polycystic" told patients — and many doctors — that the condition was about cysts on the ovaries. About 30 percent of women diagnosed with the condition don't have ovarian cysts at all, and specialists have long understood the disorder as a whole-body hormonal and metabolic condition involving insulin resistance, excess androgens and long-term cardio-metabolic risk, not just a reproductive one.

"This is not a new disorder; it's just the name correcting inaccuracies and catching up with science and patient experience."

— Professor Helena Teede, Monash Centre for Health Research and Implementation, Australia

Teede says media coverage of the rename has already reached roughly one billion people — a sharp departure for a condition long treated, in her words, as "women's secret ovary business." The reframing, she argues, moves the condition out of the narrow gynaecological category that has constrained research, education and care.

What changes, and what doesn't

The diagnostic criteria — two of three signs: irregular ovulation, excess androgens, or polycystic ovaries on ultrasound — are unchanged. Treatment is unchanged too. "The first line of treatment remains the same, it will still be medicines for improving metabolism," says Dr Manju Gupta, senior consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist at Motherhood Hospitals in Noida. Metformin and hormonal contraceptives continue — though Teede stresses patients should see them as direct hormonal treatments for the underlying disorder, not symptom-masking tools.

What may shift is the clinic visit. Dr Sulbha Arora, clinical director at Nova IVF Fertility in Mumbai, says that since many women first see a general physician, a hormonal-and-metabolic framing could bring earlier recognition: "In practical terms, there will likely be a greater emphasis on metabolic screening from the very beginning — blood sugar, lipid profiles, blood pressure, BMI assessment, and screening for fatty liver or sleep disturbances in selected patients." Teede adds there will likely be less reliance on ultrasounds in diagnosis.

The rename also changes the doctor-patient conversation: Gupta says it was long difficult to explain to young women why they were prescribed blood-sugar-lowering medicines for an "ovarian cyst" problem, and the new name should make that conversation — and compliance — easier.

Why the stakes are higher for Indian women

India carries both high prevalence and a high metabolic risk profile. "At a lower body mass index, people from India have higher metabolic complications generally and in PMOS," Teede says, pointing to elevated risks of Type 2 diabetes, gestational diabetes and heart disease. Indian women, doctors and patients had substantial input into the new framework.

The rename also carries social weight in India. Dr Aparna Govil Bhasker, a bariatric and metabolic surgeon at MetaHeal Clinic in Mumbai, says moving away from an "ovarian disease" framing could reduce the intense scrutiny Indian women face around marriageability and fertility — easing, in her words, the "blame, shame and trivialisation" attached to the condition. Several Indian public figures, including Sara Ali Khan, Sonam Kapoor, Bhumi Pednekar, Kriti Sanon, Masaba Gupta and Shruti Haasan, have spoken openly about their experiences, chipping away at the taboo.

What's next

The rename is the first of eight steps in a funded plan: rewriting medical textbooks, updating electronic health records, and — by 2028 — revising the WHO's International Classification of Diseases and treatment guidelines. Until then, Teede is candid that a woman visiting her doctor tomorrow will not get markedly different care. But for the roughly 70 percent of affected women worldwide who, per the WHO, don't know they have the condition, a name that finally describes what it is may be the first step toward being seen.
